answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — he quoted it, crediting Edmund Burke
answer.authorName: Origin unknown — long misattributed to Edmund Burke
answer.authorDates: A saying with no documented author; Burke 1729–1797
answer.sourceLine: Kennedy did speak a version of this line — “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing” — in his 17 May 1961 address to the Canadian Parliament ↗, but he introduced it as words of “the great parliamentarian Edmund Burke.” The problem is that Burke never wrote it either: as Quote Investigator ↗ documents, the saying appears nowhere in his works and its true author is unknown.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: John F. Kennedy, Address before the Canadian Parliament, Ottawa
Edmund Burke (no such line exists in Burke)

source.excerpt: As the great parliamentarian Edmund Burke said, ‘The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.’
trail: Not in Burke. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no such passage in Burke’s works; the attribution is entrenched but unsupported, and the true author is undetermined.

How it got pinned on Burke. The 14th edition of Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (1968) credited Burke, citing a 1795 letter; columnist William Safire challenged it in 1980 and the 15th edition removed the citation, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The closest real precursor. Open Culture ↗ and Wikiquote point to John Stuart Mill’s 1867 St Andrews address: “Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing.”
JFK spoke it, crediting Burke. The line appears verbatim (as “for good men to do nothing”) in his 17 May 1961 Ottawa speech ↗.
source.excerptNote: Kennedy’s exact words to the Canadian Parliament, 17 May 1961 — note he attributes the line to Burke, and that his wording is “for good men to do nothing,” a hair different from the popular “that good men do nothing.”

sourceLink.text: Kennedy’s 1961 address to the Canadian Parliament (Miller Center)

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is a saying of unknown authorship — not traceable to Burke, Mill, or Kennedy as its originator — so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for the phrase itself. (Kennedy’s 1961 speech text, where he quotes it, is a U.S. government work in the public domain, but that is a separate matter from the aphorism’s origin.)

author.name: Edmund Burke
author.heading: About the man it’s pinned on
author.bio: Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish statesman, orator and philosopher, best known for Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) and as a founder of modern conservative thought. This aphorism is the quotation most often hung on his name, yet scholars have never located it anywhere in his writings or speeches. The closest real Burke line, from his 1770 Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents, reads: “When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle.”

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most misattributed sayings in English. It is routinely credited to Edmund Burke, and increasingly to John F. Kennedy because he quoted it — but neither man originated it, and no one has established who did.

items.why: The single most common attribution, yet Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote ↗ confirm the line appears nowhere in Burke’s writings. A spurious 1795-letter citation in Bartlett’s was withdrawn after William Safire challenged it in 1980.

Kennedy did say it — in his 17 May 1961 address to the Canadian Parliament ↗ — but he explicitly credited “the great parliamentarian Edmund Burke,” so he was repeating a saying he believed was Burke’s, not authoring it.

The nearest documented precursor is Mill’s 1867 inaugural address at St Andrews: “Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing,” per Open Culture ↗ — but this is a related thought, not the popular wording.

misattribution.truthLine: The true author is unknown. The earliest close match Quote Investigator found is a 1916 speech by Rev. Charles F. Aked; the polished modern wording began being pinned on Burke around 1920, and no primary Burke source has ever surfaced — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is a fixture of speeches, yearbooks and political ads precisely because it feels authoritative — and attaching Burke’s name (or, lately, Kennedy’s) lends it the weight of a founding thinker. That borrowed authority is exactly what the record can’t support.

What survives scrutiny is more modest but more honest: a genuine Burke sentiment about good people needing to associate against bad ones (1770), a sharper Mill formulation (1867), and a 20th-century crystallization by an unknown hand that Kennedy helped make famous in 1961.
context.pull: Kennedy said it. Burke got the credit. Neither one wrote it.
